paras: The Bronx asphalt workers incident took place on 29 May 1903, when a crowd of about 300 Italian union men surrounded 26 Black laborers of the Uvalde Asphalt Company at 175th Street and Grand Concourse in The Bronx, New York City, and frightened them off the job. Police arrested four of the Italians, and the Black workers went back to work under police guard the same day. The episode is known from a single brief item in The Sun of New York.

The Black men were a gang of 26 laborers working for the Uvalde Asphalt Company under a foreman named Patrick Kelly. According to The Sun, the Italians who confronted them were union men, "while the negroes are not."

The crowd, which The Sun put at "300 strong," surrounded the crew and told them that "if they did not stop work there would be trouble." Kelly tried to drive the Italians away but failed, and the crowd frightened the Black workers into leaving. Kelly then called on Mounted Policeman Purcell, who arrested four of the Italians, after which the rest of the crowd left. No injuries were reported.

The four prisoners were arraigned before Magistrate Crane in the Morrisania police court and held in $300 bonds each for good behavior. Their names are not given, and no report of any later court action was found.

The Sun ran the story on 30 May on page 7 under the headline "Drive Negroes from Work," with the subheads "Italian Union Men Scare Asphalt Laborers" and "Four Rioters Arrested." The item called the arrested men "rioters" and explained the clash by union membership rather than race, offering no comment of its own. No other white newspaper and no Black newspaper in the coverage carried the story.
